sec.title: Replay analyses
sec.p: Building on work on human replay, as measured with MEG, in our and other research groups (e.g., Huang & Luo, 2024; Kern et al., 2024; Kurth-Nelson et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019, 2021; Nour et al., 2021; Schwartenbeck et al., 2023) we tested for the presence of two qualitatively distinct types of sequential reactivation (“sequenceness”) using temporally delayed linear modeling (TDLM). Specifically, we tested for different magnitudes of sequenceness that captured transitions between neural representations of compound stimuli (“compound sequenceness”) and condition differences of sequenceness capturing transitions between neural representations of the individual features (“factorized sequenceness”). This analysis aimed at extending previous accounts of replay compositionality (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2023; Schwartenbeck et al., 2023). In these analyses we did not detect reliable, above permutation threshold sequenceness effects during a 5-minute rest period between prior and transfer learning, neither for compound stimuli nor for individual features. Such sequenceness effects were also absent during the initial 5-minute resting period before the PRE task localizer. Additionally, we did not observe any evidence for one-step transitions between neural representations of compounds or features at rest.

We also tested an additional hypothesis regarding a potential neural mechanism supporting gradual learning, and insight-dependent, decomposition of the experienced compound stimulus sequence into underlying subprocesses. Specifically, we examined for a trial-by-trial positive linear trend for factorized sequenceness and a trial-by-trial negative linear trend for compound sequenceness during the resting period between the experience and inference probe question (inter-probe intervals). Again, we did not detect significant and reliable sequenceness effects.

The absence of sequential reactivation findings in these data may relate to several factors. Firstly, we optimized hyper-parameters and classifier performance on visual localizer tasks and tested their generalization on memory reactivation during “no-task” resting periods. The L1-regularization training procedure minimizes an overlap between representations of visually presented stimuli by reducing the magnitude of regression weights for non-influential sensors. Conceivably, this might impede an ability to reliably detect memory reactivation during “no-task” resting periods, rendering quantification of sequential memory reactivation challenging. Secondly, it is possible that the compositional generalization behavior seen in the present task may not rely on “offline” sequential reactivation of experienced task states. The behaviorally relevant information to be learned by participants encompassed one-step transitions between compound states (and features) alone, potentially rendering underpowered any sequential reactivation analyses that relies on multiple-step transitions of reactivated states.

sec.title: Successor feature prediction
sec.p: This analysis aimed at assessing evidence for neural representation of successor features in both subprocesses.

We employed L1-regularized (LASSO) logistic regression classifiers to MEG data recorded during stimulus presentations in the PRE task localizer and transfer learning phase. Individually optimized L1 penalty hyper-parameter values (λ) per participant were obtained using leave-one-run-out cross-validation (5-fold CV, training on four of the localizer blocks and testing classifier performance on the remaining block) individually on neural activity recorded at all individually presented transfer learning phase features during the PRE task localizer. Optimized hyper-parameters were used to train classifiers per participant on the transfer learning phase features presented during the PRE task localizer. Since we employed a one vs all classification scheme and every compound stimulus presented during the transfer learning phase was composed of two features, we reasoned that the classifier representing the other (irrelevant) feature in the compound stimulus would show the highest predicted probability. We sought to control for the confounding influence of the other stimulus (of no interest) contained in the compound stimulus by training and testing classifiers excluding the respective other stimulus, resulting in n * n-1 (10 * 9 = 90) classifiers. We then applied the trained classifiers to test their generalization abilities in the transfer learning phase – generating the predicted probability for each successor feature for each subprocess separately, on each compound stimulus presentation. Since all classifiers showed some level of predicted probability, we used the raw predicted probability as a neural metric of successor state representation (instead of computing the classification accuracy for the next state only). No cross-validation was performed since training and testing were performed on independent datasets.

We analyzed neural activity in a time window from 0 – 800 ms post-stimulus onset for each presented compound stimulus. This interval was chosen since the PRE task localizer presented each stimulus for 650 ms. The 800 ms post-stimulus period was shorter than the 1000 ms image display duration in transfer learning – we therefore make no claims about successor state reactivations that might have potentially occurred between 800 and 1000 ms post-stimulus onset.

To quantify the neural representation of successor features, we subtracted the averaged pre-stimulus onset (−200 – 0 ms) predicted probabilities on a given stimulus presentation from the post-stimulus predicted probabilities – providing a neural metric for feature reactivation. We conducted one-sample t-tests against 0 (null effect) predicted probability, jointly for both prior learning conditions at each time point post-stimulus onset for Component 4 and Component 6 subprocess successor feature representation. We then identified contiguous clusters of time points where the observed t-values exceeded a predefined threshold (critical t-value) and computed the sum of t-values within each cluster. To correct for multiple comparisons, we performed a cluster-based permutation procedure with 1000 permutations. In each permutation, we shuffled the sign of each of the successor feature activations before recomputing the t-values vs 0 at each time point. We then identified contiguous clusters of time points where the observed t-values exceeded a predefined threshold and used the largest cluster-level t-sum from each permutation to build an empirical null distribution.

An empirical p-value was computed by counting the number of times the original cluster sum was greater than or equal to the permuted t-sums. A cluster in the observed data was deemed significant family-wise error corrected at the cluster-level if the empirical p-value was PFWE < 0.05.

sec.title: Cross-phase representational similarity analysis
sec.p: Complementary to the decoding analysis in Figure 4, we conducted a cross-phase representational similarity analysis (RSA) to test whether neural representations of central nodes were stable across their distinct serial positions within a sequence, a property expected under abstract structural role coding but not under serial position coding. We focused on central nodes of the 6-state graph, as these nodes appear twice within each sequence traversal of the bridge graph: the left central node occurs at steps 1 and 4, the right central node occurs at steps 5 and 8, allowing first and second presentations to be dissociated.

Structural roles were assigned separately for prior and transfer learning phases. For line graphs (experienced by the Condition 4 during prior learning), central nodes were identified from node degree in the adjacency matrix (boundary: degree 1; intermediate: neighbors of boundary; central: remaining nodes), and the two central nodes were ordered by first appearance in the trial list. For bridge graphs, central nodes were identified from the predefined 8-step traversal template.

At each time point and sensor, condition-specific activations were estimated using occurrence-specific GLMs: one GLM fitted to trials corresponding to the first occurrence of each number in the trial list, and one fitted to trials corresponding to the second occurrence. Component 6-specific beta estimates were extracted from each GLM separately, yielding four sets of neural patterns per subject: prior-phase first occurrence, prior-phase second occurrence, transfer-phase first occurrence, and transfer-phase second occurrence.

Cross-phase representational dissimilarity was then computed using an L1 distance metric (mean absolute difference across sensors) across four cross-presentation pairs: Left central (prior first, transfer second), left central (prior second, transfer first), right central (prior first, transfer second), and right central (prior second, transfer first). These pairings compare the same node across different serial positions and different learning phases, directly controlling for time-in-sequence as a potential confound. The mean L1 distance across the four pairs constituted the cross-presentation dissimilarity index at each time point, where lower values indicate greater neural similarity. Timecourses were baseline-corrected by subtracting the pre-stimulus mean (timepoints 1–25, corresponding to −250 to 0 ms) per participant, and analyses were restricted to post-stimulus timepoints. Group differences between Condition 6 and Condition 4 participants were assessed using a two-sample non-parametric cluster permutation test (cluster-forming threshold p = 0.10, cluster-level alpha = 0.05, 1,000 permutations, one-tailed, consistent with the directional prediction that Condition 6 participants would show greater cross-phase neural similarity for central nodes). The results are presented in Supplementary Figure 4.

body.p: This study provides valuable insights into humans' ability to generalize learned structural knowledge to new experiences that share underlying graph components but involve different stimuli. The behavioral and MEG evidence is solid, broadly supporting the transfer of abstract structural knowledge across contexts, although the findings speak more directly to the reuse of individual structural components than to their recombination. This study will be of interest to cognitive neuroscientists studying structure learning, abstract representations, and the generalization of knowledge across contexts.
Summary:

The paper presents an elegant task designed to investigate humans' ability to generalize knowledge of learned graph structures to new experiences that share the same structure but are built from different stimuli. Using behavior and MEG recordings, the authors test evidence for neural representation and application of structural knowledge.
Comments on revised version.

The authors have addressed my concerns and have largely toned-down the overstatement of their findings which was pervasive in the previous version of the manuscript. However, the revised title still seems rather misleading given the findings presented. I suggest the authors revise this to: 'A neural mechanism for transfer of abstract structural knowledge in humans'.

The authors track structural role representations during stimulus processing, which is relevant to study how prior experience shapes new learning. They employ a sequence learning task based on graph factorization and record brain activity using MEG to investigate whether graph factors are reused during learning and inference in a new graph. MEG data were recorded during passive stimulus presentation, while behavior is assessed in a subset of probe trials testing either experienced or inferred successions in the graph. The authors report neural similarity among stimuli conditional on their role in subprocesses, and a correlation between evidence for role representations and performance in experience probes, but not in inference probes.

The interpretation of "knowledge transfer" in the title and abstract is, however, constrained by the absence of a corresponding relationship with performance in the inference probes, which provide the behavioral measure of transfer. While the authors discuss why role representations might relate more closely to experience than inference probes in this task, this distinction makes the link between the neural findings and transfer weaker than the current framing suggests. (E.g., "was positively related to behavioral success in subprocess knowledge transfer" in the abstract could be misleading)

More broadly, the framing of the results as a mechanism for structure transfer or structural scaffolding appears stronger than warranted by the evidence. The findings indicate representations consistent with reusable roles, but do not establish that these representations functionally facilitate learning and transfer. The claims should align with this distinction between evidence for representational reuse and structural scaffolding.
Also, apart from abstract roles, simpler categorical grouping of different stimuli belonging to the same subprocess could produce increased similarity.

Relatedly, although the MEG-behavior (experience probes) correlation is significant for Component 6 but not Component 4, the difference between the two correlations is not significant. Interpreting the correlation as selective to the structurally relevant graph is thus difficult to statistically substantiate.

Overall, the study provides a well-designed paradigm for investigating compositional representations during structural generalization at high temporal resolution. However, the findings do not provide sufficient evidence to frame them as a mechanism for structure transfer.
Summary:

This study investigates how task components can be learned and transferred across different task contexts. The authors designed two consecutive sequence learning tasks, in which complex image sequences were generated from the combination of two graph-based structural "building blocks". One of these components was shared between the prior and transfer task environments, allowing the authors to test compositional transfer. Behavioral analyses using generalized linear models (GLMs) assessed participants' sensitivity to the underlying structure. MEG data were recorded and analyzed using classifications and feature representational similarity analysis (RSA) to examine whether neural similarity increased for stimuli sharing the same relational structure. The paper aims to uncover the neural dynamics that support compositional transfer during learning.
Strengths and weaknesses:

I found the methods and task design of this paper difficult to follow, particularly the way stimuli were constructed and how the experimental sequences were generated from the graph structures. These aspects would be hard to replicate without some clarification. I appreciate the integration of behavioral and neuroimaging data. The overall approach, especially the use of compositional graph structures in sequence learning, is interesting and could be used and revised in further studies in compositionality and transfer learning. I appreciated the authors' careful interpretation of their findings in the discussion. However, I would have liked a similar level of caution in the abstract, which currently overstates some claims.
Comments on revised version.
No further comments. I thank the authors for their diligence in addressing my comments.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

However, the evidence for the authors' claims is incomplete, with the main claims of structural generalization and compositionality only partially supported by MEG and behavioral data. This study will be of interest to cognitive neuroscientists studying structure learning and generalization.

disp-quote.p: Summary of the paper:

The paper presents an elegant task designed to investigate humans' ability to generalize knowledge of learned graph structures to new experiences that share the same structure but are built from different stimuli. Using behavior and MEG recordings, the authors test evidence for neural representation and application of structural knowledge.

body.p: We appreciate this overall positive evaluation of our work and suggestions to strengthen the empirical support for the claims made in the paper.

disp-quote.p: (1) While the task design is elegant, it isn't clear to me that the data support all the claims made in the paper. I have detailed my concerns below.

The authors claim that their findings reveal "striking learning and generalization abilities based on factorization of complex experiences into underlying structural elements, parsing these into distinct sub processes derived from past experience, and forming a representation of the dynamical roles these features play within distinct subprocesses." And "neural dynamics that support compositional generalisation, consistent with a structural scaffolding mechanism that facilitates efficient adaption within new contexts".

(a) First, terms used in these example quotes (but also throughout the paper) do not seem to be well supported by data or the task design. For example, terms such as 'compositional generalisation' and 'building blocks' have important relevance in other papers by (some of) the same authors (e.g., Schwartenbeck et al., 2023), but in the context of this experiment, what is 'composition'?

body.p: We agree that our use of composition is less technical and formal than the nested and recursive forms of composition using “building blocks” reported in previous work (e.g., Schwartenbeck et al., 2023). In this experiment we study composition of smaller graphs via superimposition of their outputs. The superimposed “compound” outputs can be viewed as outputs of a single, more complex, graph. This is a special case of all possible ways that graphs can be composed from other graphs, and does not depend on a complex syntax for their combination (although more complex combination rules, other than multiplication are theoretically possible). Nevertheless, in accordance with common definitions of compositionality, this leads to a generative setup, given that a huge number of graphs can be expressed as the product of smaller graphs in this way.

Figure panel (Fig 1A) illustrates this precise point. Importantly, we argue this kind of composition is ubiquitous in real-world learning scenarios where multiple independent processes contribute to the holistic experience of a situation.
Based on the reviewer’s suggestion we have now amended the manuscript introduction to render the distinction between different definitions, and usage, of the term composition more salient.

It is our understanding that this form of flexible, combinatorial, reuse of factorized prior knowledge is considered a specific instance of composition. Indeed, this understanding is supported by a cognitive-computational neuroscience literature that adheres to similar conceptualizations of compositionality, e.g., Barron et al., 2013 Nat Neuro; Rubino et al., 2023 PsyArxiv; Luettgau et al., 2024 PNAS.
We add a paragraph to the introduction section elaborating on what we mean by graph factorization and its relevance for questions of compositional generalization (reproduced below for convenience).

To address these questions, we developed a sequence learning paradigm based on a graph theoretical concept of graph factorization, emulating environments whose dynamics are the product of multiple simultaneous subprocesses. “Product graphs (Cartesian product), wherein the joint dynamics of two or more graph factors create complex product state space dynamics that can be factorized (and simplified) into constitutive factors, provides a compelling and flexible test bed for probing compositional generalization of multiple (independent) and simultaneously unfolding subprocesses.” Examples of such graph products and their factorizations, from a vast space of possible combinations, are provided in Figure 1A. Here we take inspiration from prior studies in neuroscience (e.g., Barron et al., 2013; Rubino et al., 2023; Schwartenbeck et al., 2023) and a prior cognitive literature, e.g., recursive operations over hierarchies (O’Donnell et al., 2009, 2011), hierarchical function composition, or rich forms of semantic composition in language to create complex concepts (Murphy, 1988).

disp-quote.p: (2) Can the authors demonstrate clear behavioural or neural evidence for compositional use of multiple graph structures, or alternatively remove reference to these terms? In the current paper, it seems to me that the authors are investigating abstract knowledge for singular graph structures (together with the influence of prior learning), as opposed to knowledge for the compound, more complex graph formed from the product of two simpler graphs.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important clarification, and agree our language should more precisely distinguish what the task design requires from what our data directly demonstrate. The reviewer is correct that our analyses primarily provide evidence for the abstraction and transfer of a single previously-experienced graph structure to novel stimuli, rather than direct evidence that participants combine two independently learned structures into a novel compound representation. We agree this distinction is important, and we have revised our language throughout the manuscript accordingly, reserving "compositional generalization" to describe the broader task structure (in which every compound stimulus is the joint product of two simultaneously evolving subprocesses, and the specific compound experienced during transfer learning was never observed during prior learning) and using more precise language: "decomposition," "abstraction," and "transfer" of single structural components to describe what our behavioral and neural evidence actually establishes. We have not claimed direct evidence that participants compositionally construct novel joint representations from two previously separate structures; rather, our evidence concerns the selective reuse of one such component when it recurs across learning phases, embedded in a novel pairing with another, entirely new structural component. We have adjusted the manuscript throughout and changed the title of the paper to “A neural mechanism for compositional structure transfer in humans”, to more adequately reflect the evidence presented.

disp-quote.p: (3) While I would like to be convinced that this data provides evidence for the transfer of abstract, structural knowledge, I think the authors either need to provide more convincing evidence or tone down their claims.

Can the increase in neural similarity between stimuli mapping to the same abstract structural sub-process not be explained by temporal proximity in experiencing the transitions (e.g., Cai et al., 2016)? Indeed, behavior seems to be dominated by direct experience of the structure as opposed to applying abstract knowledge of equivalent structures (and, as a result, there is little difference in behavioural performance between experience and inference probes).

body.p: The reviewer makes an astute observation while providing a constructive challenge. We agree that distinguishing transfer of abstract structural knowledge from effects driven by direct temporal experience is critical, and we appreciate this opportunity to clarify our reasoning on this point.

The reviewer suggests that increased neural similarity between stimuli that map to the same abstract structural sub-process might be explained by a temporal proximity in experience, as shown in prior work (e.g., Cai et al., 2016). We agree that temporal proximity is a potentially powerful determinant of representational similarity. Likewise, we do not dispute that temporal statistics of experience play an important role in shaping such neural representations. Nevertheless, we believe these accounts do not provide a sufficient explanation for our results, which we consider reflects a consequence of being exposed to the outputs produced by sequences drawn from an underlying graph structure and a prior learning of these sequences.

In our task, the temporal statistics of stimulus experience are fully dictated by the transition structure of the graph. Different graph structures necessarily impose different constraints on temporal proximity (e.g., how many steps it takes to revisit a given node, which nodes are encountered at similar temporal distances, etc.). Thus, if stimuli that occupy equivalent structural roles across different graphs come to be represented more similarly, this is precisely because learners have abstracted over the specific transition structure that governs these temporal relationships. In other words, consistent with our previous computational findings that models based on temporal difference learning mechanisms account well for behavioural response patterns (Luettgau et al., 2024 PNAS), temporal proximity is not a confound but instead is a likely mechanism through which structural knowledge is acquired. Critically, our key claims concern transfer across learning contexts, and not sensitivity to temporal proximity within a single experience stream. By design, the selective learning improvements observed in each group during transfer cannot be explained by temporal proximity alone, because the relevant temporal statistics in the transfer phase are novel and differ across groups. The fact that prior learning selectively facilitates subsequent learning depending on an earlier experience of an abstract structure indicates participants are not simply tracking local temporal regularities, but instead are reusing previously learned structural knowledge to guide learning within a new context.

We agree that behavior in our task is strongly influenced by direct experience, and we do not claim that participants rely exclusively on abstract structural knowledge. Indeed, the relatively small differences between experience and inference probes are consistent with the view that abstraction complements and facilitates, rather than replaces, learning from direct experience. Our claims are therefore deliberately modest: we argue for the transfer of abstract structural knowledge that shapes learning dynamics and neural representations, not for behavior dominated by explicit inference over abstract graphs.

To avoid any criticism related to over-interpretation, we have toned down our language and clarify throughout introduction, results and discussion section of the manuscript that (i) temporal proximity is an intrinsic feature of graph structure, (ii) neural effects reflect (in part) abstraction over these structured temporal relationships, and (iii) that our results provide evidence for transfer of structural knowledge that biases learning, rather than for fully context-independent representations or strong behavioral generalization.

disp-quote.p: (4) The strongest evidence for neural representation of abstract task structures seems to be the increase in similarity by transition type. But this common code for 'transition type' is only observed for 6-bridge graphs and only for experienced transitions. There was no significant effect in inference probes. Therefore, there doesn't seem to be evidence for the application of a knowledge scaffold to facilitate transfer learning. Instead, the data reflects learning from direct experience and not generalisation.

body.p: We appreciate the reviewer's point, and agree it deserves a careful investigation. We carefully considered how this correlation could be interpreted under a non-transfer, pure direct-experience account. Our interpretation is that even if all graph learning relies entirely on direct experience, a correlation is still expected due to individual differences in learning ability. Under this framework, higher-ability participants are simply more likely to directly discover the same structural component (the 6-bridge) across both sessions (prior and transfer learning), which in turn supports higher MEG transition decodability. Concurrently, these same participants will exhibit higher behavioral accuracy due to their superior learning capacity. Importantly, under this account, these higher-ability participants should also show higher behavioural accuracy during the transfer phase for the 4-cycle component, predicting (a) a positive correlation between our transition decoding signal and 4-cycle behavioural accuracy, and (b) a positive correlation between 4-cycle and 6-bridge behavioural accuracy themselves, within each prior learning group.

We tested both predictions directly. For (a), in the 6-bridge prior group, average decoding strength at timepoints showing a selective significant group difference correlated with experience probe performance on the 6-bridge graph during transfer learning (ρ = .48, p = .016, surviving correction for two comparisons, α = .025), but the corresponding correlation with 4-cycle behavioural accuracy did not reach significance (ρ = .38, p = .071). We acknowledge, however, that a direct comparison of these two dependent correlations (Steiger's test) did not reach significance (p = .66).

For (b), we directly correlated 4-cycle and 6-bridge transfer accuracy within each prior learning group. For experience probes, this correlation was significant in the 4-cycle prior group (ρ = .51, p = .010) but not in the 6-bridge prior group (ρ = .24, p = .257); for inference probes, the pattern reversed, with a significant correlation in the 6-bridge prior group (ρ = .42, p = .035) but not the 4-cycle prior group (ρ = .16, p = .452). In neither probe type did a direct comparison of the two groups' correlation coefficients reach significance (experience probes: Z = -1.06, p = .291; inference probes: Z = .95, p = .340). Given that two of these four single-group correlations were nominally significant (without correction for multiple comparisons) while the corresponding between-group comparisons were not, and given the inconsistency in which group/probe-type combination shows the effect, we consider this pattern inconclusive rather than supportive of a clear general-ability signal linking performance on the two graph components.

We therefore cannot statistically rule out the general-ability account with the current sample, and have revised our interpretation accordingly: rather than claiming strict specificity to the 6-bridge structure, we now describe the correlation as selective to 6-bridge experience probes in this sample, while acknowledging that distinguishing structural reuse from a more general learning ability to represent novel relational structure remains an open question. We have added the decoding-strength comparison as a new Supplementary Figure 5, showing decoding-strength correlations with both 4-state and 6-bridge graph performance side by side, and report the direct behavioural correlation between graph components in the text, and have revised the relevant main-text passage to match these updated values.

We also wish to address why this correlation was selective to experience probes and did not extend to inference probes. We agree that, under an assumption of perfectly learned and context-independent abstract representations, one might expect performance on experience and inference probes to relate equally to the decoding signal. We believe the reviewer's concern is valid only under an assumption of perfect abstraction. In our task, abstract roles correspond to latent structural variables that are learned gradually and with uncertainty. Under such conditions, role inference is inherently context-dependent: the role of a given stimulus is not inferred in isolation, but in relation to the compound within which it appears. For example, if one element of a compound is already known with high confidence to belong to a particular subgraph, the role of the second element can be inferred more reliably; in contrast, when both elements are themselves uncertain, role inference becomes less precise. Critically, learning is unlikely to be uniform across compounds, as structural knowledge may be acquired with variable precision for different stimulus pairings depending on their frequency, co-occurrence statistics, and position within a sequence. This variability in learning precision means we would expect corresponding variability in a participant's ability to infer dynamical roles across different compound types, and consequently in their ability to make accurate predictions about those compounds. Under this account, our MEG signal, which indexes role-based representational structure specifically for experienced compounds, most directly reflects knowledge precision for those items; a correlation with inference probe accuracy requires an additional inferential step from experienced to novel compounds, introducing noise proportional to uncertainty in the underlying learned representations. We have revised the Discussion to make this reasoning more explicit.

disp-quote.p: (5) The authors frequently suggest that they are providing insight into temporal dynamics, but there is no mention of particular oscillations or particular temporal sequences of neural representation that support task performance.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this. We agree our use of the term "temporal dynamics" is potentially misleading, and we have now revised the manuscript accordingly. Our analyses did set out to identify specific neural oscillations, rhythmic processes, or temporally ordered stages of computation that support task performance. Rather, time-resolved MEG analyses is a method that allows us to track when representational content is expressed during stimulus processing, serving three research questions about subprocess-specific representational similarity, dynamical role representations, and relationship to behavioral transfer performance; as opposed to characterizing the temporal organization of underlying computations per se.

We have now removed or replaced references to "temporal dynamics" and "neural dynamics" throughout the manuscript where these might be interpreted as claims about oscillatory or sequentially structured neural mechanisms. Instead, we now frame our conclusions in terms of representational content and its modulation by prior learning experience. We believe this aligns our language with what the data actually support and removes potential confusion regarding the scope of our claims.

disp-quote.p: (6) Regardless of point (b), can the authors provide more convincing evidence for a graph structure being represented per se (regardless of whether this representation is directly experienced or inferred)? From Figure 3C, it seems that the model RDM doesn't account for relative distance within the graph. Do they see evidence for distance coding? Can they reconstruct the graph from representational patterns using MDS?

body.p: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. The reviewer is correct that the model RDM shown in (previous) Figure 3C does not specifically capture relative distance within the graph and asks whether there is evidence for distance coding or whether the graph can be reconstructed using techniques such as MDS. We agree that distance-based representations are one possible signature of graph knowledge, with such effects reported in a prior literature. However, our theoretical focus is on an investigation of a more functionally relevant aspect of graph structure learning and reuse of abstracted knowledge: the representation of graph nodes according to their structural roles or positions within a graph.

To address the question more directly, we ran an additional sensor-level RSA analysis using the localizer task data, comparing representational changes from PRE to POST learning. Specifically, we examined whether stimuli in the 6-bridge graph that map onto the same structural roles (e.g., boundary, intermediate, central) within the relevant graph structures show greater neural similarity from before to after learning, and whether this effect depends on the graph structure experienced during prior learning. This new analysis revealed a cluster-based, permutation-corrected, interaction effect between prior learning group and graph factor, consistent with a representational similarity increase selectively for stimuli sharing the same structural role in a graph structure relevant to each group’s prior experience. Importantly, this effect occurs at similar time points as our earlier RSA effects based on overall stimulus-set similarity, suggesting that both analyses capture related aspects of the same underlying representational processes.

We believe this role-based representational similarity provides more direct evidence for graph-structured representations and their transfer across learning than distance-based or MDS reconstructions in our task context. First, distance within the graph is necessarily correlated with temporal proximity of experience, making it difficult to disentangle distance coding from local transition statistics. Second, multiple distinct graph structures used in our experiment (e.g., cycles, lines, and bridges) share overlapping distance relationships but differ in their higher-order structural roles. Our analysis therefore targets those aspects of structure that are invariant across surface features and that are most relevant for transfer across learning contexts.

For these reasons, while we do not claim we can reconstruct full graph geometry from neural patterns, our results are consistent with an organization of neural representations according to abstract structural positions within a graph, that is independent of specific stimulus identities. We have added a new panel to Figure 3 illustrating this role-based RSA effect and also expanded the Methods and Results sections to describe this analysis in detail. We believe this addition provides more convincing evidence that participants represent graph structure at an abstract level, even when that structure is not explicitly experienced in the same form during the localiser task. We thank the reviewer for encouraging this more specific analysis, as it significantly strengthens our claims.

“To test whether localiser representations of abstract graph structure generalised across sets experienced in the main task, we performed RSA separately for PRE and POST localisers. Structural roles were derived from each participant’s learning-phase transition sequences. For 4-state graphs, nodes were assigned to two matched role bins (boundary-like vs central-like) based on first-encounter order within each phase. For 6-state graphs, roles were determined either from node degree (6-line: boundary, intermediate, central). For 6-bridge graphs we used a predefined structural template. Specifically, the first eight valid transitions in the learning phase were mapped onto a fixed sequence of structural roles (central–intermediate–boundary–central–central–intermediate–boundary–central). Each node was assigned a role based on the majority role it occupied across its occurrences in these eight steps (ties resolved in favour of central > intermediate > boundary). For the localiser data, at each time point and sensor we estimated condition-specific activations using a GLM with 20 dummy-coded regressors (10 identities × 2 sets). This yielded sensor-wise beta patterns for each condition. Cross-set representational dissimilarities were computed using an L1 distance metric (mean absolute difference across sensors), resulting in 4×4 and 6×6 cross-set RDMs at each time point. We then summarised each RDM according to structural role: within-role distances (same role across sets), between-role distances (different roles), and their difference (delta = between − within). To control for unequal pair counts, between-role comparisons were subsampled to match the number of within-role pairs (200 repetitions). This produced time-resolved structural generalisation indices for 4-state and 6-state graphs, which were submitted to group-level statistical analyses as described above.”

disp-quote.p: (7) In general, the figures are not very clear, and the outcome from statistical tests is not graphically shown. The paper would be easier to digest if, for example, Figures 1-2 were made clearer and statistical significance relative to chance were indicated throughout. To give two examples: (i) Figure 1 should clearly indicate what is meant by observed and held-out transitions and whether it is just the transition or also the compound that is new to the participant. (ii) Figure 2D-E could be shown with relevant comparisons and simpler statistical comparisons. Currently, it is hard to follow without carefully reading the legend.

body.p: We have taken the reviewer’s point on board and have revised the figures to improve clarity. Specifically, we have improved labeling and visual annotation in Figure 1 to clearly distinguish observed versus held-out transitions and to highlight the key experimental manipulations. We have also simplified the presentation of behavioral results in Figure 2D–E and made the most relevant statistical comparisons more explicit, with statistical outcomes now indicated directly in the figures where appropriate.

We believe these changes improve readability and reduce the burden on the reader, while still relying on the figure captions to convey essential methodological details and interpretation, following standard practice. See Figure 1 and Figure 2.

disp-quote.p: (1) For the classifier: what was the overall accuracy of the classifier when tested on held-out examples of the same stimuli? Relative to chance? Relative to entirely different stimuli that have the same transition type (e.g., line 424)?
(2) In the Results paragraph 2 can you state how many subjects had prior exposure to 4-state vs how many had prior exposure to 6-state?

body.p: This has now been added these data to the results section, reproduced below for convenience:

In brief, participants “(N = 50, N = 25 subjects per condition)” performed a sequence learning task, observing image sequences produced by walks on product graphs constructed from smaller graph factors (Fig. 1A and B).

disp-quote.p: Summary:

The authors aimed to investigate the temporal dynamics of how prior experiences shape learning in new complex environments by examining whether the brain reuses abstract structural components from those experiences. They employed a sequence learning task based on graph factorization and recorded neural activity using magnetoencephalography (MEG) to investigate how the underlying graph factors are reused to support learning and inference in a new graph. MEG data was derived from passive stimulus presentation trials, and behavior was assessed through a small number of probe trials testing either experienced or inferred successions in the graph. Representational similarity analysis of the MEG data was performed at a quite aggregated level (the principal components explaining 80% of the variance). The authors report (1) enhanced neural similarity among stimuli that belong to the same graph-factor as well as (2) a correlation between abstract role representations, corresponding to particular positions in the graph, and performance in experience-probes but not in inference-probes.

Overall, the findings are congruent with prior research on neural correlates of structural abstraction. They offer an elegant, well-suited task design to study compositional representations, replicating the authors' earlier finding and providing temporal information on structural generalisation in a sequence learning task.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this positive evaluation of our work and insightful comments and suggestions.

disp-quote.p: (1) The first finding is considered evidence for representational alignment of the graph factors. However, alignment seems to be just one possible arrangement underlying the increased similarity between stimuli of the same vs different graph factors. For instance, a simple categorical grouping of stimuli belonging to the same graph, rather than their structural alignment, could also underlie the reported effect. The wording should be adjusted to avoid over interpretation.

body.p: We agree with the reviewer that increased neural similarity between stimuli associated with the same graph factor does not uniquely imply representational alignment in its strongest sense, and could in principle also reflect a more general categorical grouping of stimuli based solely on belonging to the same graph. We revised the manuscript to tone down the wording and avoid overinterpretation, replacing references to “representational alignment” with more neutral language that refers to increased within-factor representational similarity.

At the same time, we believe that additional analyses introduced in the revised manuscript constrain alternative accounts. In particular, our new analysis on localiser data, examining representational changes from PRE to POST learning for stimuli that map onto the same structural roles within relevant sub-process graph structures. This analysis showed the presence of a cluster-based, permutation-corrected, interaction effect between group and graph factor, indicating that representational similarity increases selectively for stimuli sharing the same structural role, rather than simply increased similarity for all stimuli associated with the same graph.

Because these role-based groupings cut across specific stimulus identities and cannot be reduced to a single categorical label for an entire graph, we believe this result provides specific evidence that neural representations are shaped by internal structural properties of the graph, rather than reflecting the emergence of a coarse categorical distinction between graph types. We have added this analysis as a new panel to Figure 3 and expanded the Results and Methods sections accordingly (reproduced below for convenience):

“The observed increase in neural similarity between stimuli associated with the same graph factor could, in principle, reflect a more general categorical grouping of stimuli belonging to the same graph factor, rather than reflecting an abstract graph representation. To address this alternative account, we examined whether neural similarity in the localizer task is specifically structured according to the graph-theoretic role each stimulus occupies within its graph, using a finer-grained theoretical RDM that distinguishes between boundary, intermediate, and central positions. Structural roles were derived from each participant's learning task sequences and defined by graph topology. For Component 6, roles were assigned using a bridge-graph traversal template (for Condition 6, whose prior learning involved the bridge graph) or degree-based assignment (for Condition 4, whose prior learning involved a line graph): boundary nodes were defined as nodes with degree 1 (graph periphery); intermediate nodes as neighbours of boundary nodes; and central nodes as the remaining, more densely connected nodes. For Component 4, two roles were distinguished, boundary-like nodes (those encountered first and last in the sequence traversal) and central-like nodes (those encountered second and third), reflecting structural position within the graph rather than arbitrary temporal sequence. For further details of role assignment, see Methods. This analysis revealed a cluster-based permutation-corrected interaction (PFEW < 0.05, non-parametric permutation test, Figure 3E) between prior learning group and graph factor at overlapping time windows with the previously reported PCA and sensor-level analyses investigating feature-mappings to abstract graph factors. We did not observe significant and multiple comparisons corrected prior learning group and graph factor main effects (all PFEW > 0.90, non-parametric permutation test). These results indicate that representational similarity increased selectively for stimuli sharing the same structural role in the graph structure relevant to each group’s prior experience. Critically, this effect was not observed uniformly for all stimuli associated with the same graph, arguing against a purely categorical grouping explanation. Instead, these findings provide evidence that learning induces representations that reflect higher-order relational structure, capturing graph-theoretic roles that are invariant across surface features of the embedding stimuli and support transfer across learning contexts.

Taken together, our findings indicate a task-induced, learning-related increase in neural similarity for stimuli sharing a structural role in subprocesses common across task phases and is compatible with a structural scaffolding mechanism, though we do not claim these representations are fully context-independent.

disp-quote.p: (2) The second finding of abstract role representations is indeed expected for structural generalisation. While the data presents an interesting indication, its interpretability is constrained by a lack of testing for generalization of the effect to other graph structures (e.g., to rule out graph-specific strategies) as well as the absence of a link to transfer performance in inference-probes. The authors argue that the experienced transitions the classifier was trained on might be more similar in process to the experience-probes than the inference-probes. However, as inference-probes are the key measure of transfer, one could argue that if abstract role representations truly underlie transfer learning, they should be evident in the common neural signal.

body.p: The reviewer provides a thoughtful comment and we agree that, under an assumption of perfectly learned and context-independent abstract representations, one might expect this would be related equally to performance in experience and inference probes. Below, we clarify the scope of our claims, including presenting additional neural evidence for abstract role representations, and argue that an absence of a strong neural-behavioral correlation for inference probes is not inconsistent with our proposed abstract structural knowledge account of transfer learning.

First, we acknowledge that our experiment tests generalization only across two graph families, rather than across a broader set of graph structures. While we think it unlikely that our findings are idiosyncratic to cycles or bridge-like graphs, a we now limit our claims and emphasise a future need for testing generalization across additional graph families (see discussion section as reproduced below)

“We concede that the present experiment examines generalization across two families of graph structures, rather than across a broader space of possible graphs. While we consider it unlikely that our findings are idiosyncratic to cycles, lines and bridge-like graphs, we acknowledge that further work will be needed to support abstraction beyond the limited graph structures studied here.”

Second, to provide more direct neural evidence that abstract structural roles within the studied graphs are represented per se, we add a new analysis that uses independent localizer task data. In this analysis, we performed a sensor-level RSA contrasting pre- and post-learning representations. Specifically, we test whether stimuli that occupied the same role within learned graph substructures became more neurally similar after learning. This localizer RSA revealed a cluster-corrected interaction effect between prior learning group and graph factor, expressed in an increased representational similarity for stimuli mapping onto equivalent structural roles, independent of specific stimulus identities and outside the task context of the main learning phase. This result supports the proposal that participants form abstract, role-based, representations of graph structure where these representations are not tied to a particular transition sequence or probe type. This finding adds an important insight in that it goes beyond establishing role representations for the 6-bridge graph factor, enabling us to make claims about generalization of structural knowledge of the 4-cycle graph factor in the 4-cycle prior condition (thereby to some extent showing a wider generalization across more structural forms).

For 4-state graphs, nodes were assigned to two matched role bins (boundary-like vs central-like) based on first-encounter order within each phase.
